 1              Pursuant to Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 16 and 26, Civil Local Rule 16-9, the Standing

 2   Order for All Judges of the Northern District of California, the Court’s Standing Order for Civil

 3   Cases, and the Court’s Order on January 9, 2025 (Dkt. 38) (as adjusted by the clerk’s notice on

 4   June 2, 2025 (Dkt. 87)), counsel for Plaintiff Musi Inc. (“Musi”) and counsel for Defendant Apple

 5   Inc. (“Apple,” and collectively with Musi, the “Parties”), have met and conferred on certain issues

 6   and respectfully submit this Joint Case Management Statement in advance of the case management

 7   conference scheduled for July 30, 2025, at 10:00 a.m. 1

 8              1. Jurisdiction and Service

 9              The Parties agree that the Court has subject matter jurisdiction over Musi’s claims under
10   28 U.S.C. §1332(a) (diversity jurisdiction) because Musi is a foreign corporation with citizenship
11   different from Apple, an American corporation. The Parties further agree that the Court has
12   general personal jurisdiction over Apple because it is headquartered in California, and Apple was
13   properly served with the Complaint on October 4, 2024. No other parties remain to be served.
14   Venue is appropriate in this District under 28 U.S.C. § 1391(b) because Apple transacts business
15   within this District and participates in interstate trade and commerce in this District.
16              2. Facts
17              Musi’s Position:
18              Musi is a mobile computing software company that owns and operates the Musi app, an
19   iOS-based mobile application. The Musi app provides users with enhanced functionality to
20   interact with publicly available content on YouTube’s website through Musi’s proprietary user
21   interface components and organizational features. Importantly, the Musi app does not rely on
22   YouTube’s Application Programming Interface (“API”), nor do Musi’s servers store, process, or
23   transmit YouTube videos. Instead, the app plays or displays content based on the user’s own
24   interactions with YouTube and enhances the user experience via Musi’s proprietary technology.
25

26

27   1
         Apple’s motion for sanctions (Dkt. 79) will also be heard on July 30, 2025.
28
         Case No. 5:24-cv-06920-EKL                     2                  JOINT CASE MANAGEMENT STATEMENT
             Case 5:24-cv-06920-EKL         Document 91        Filed 07/16/25     Page 3 of 18




 1   Contrary to Apple’s assertions, Musi does not interfere with or replace any ads to the extent they

 2   are included within the publicly available video media streamed by a Musi user.

 3           Since at least 2015, Musi has engaged in periodic dialogue with YouTube, consistently

 4   expressing its commitment to offer the Musi app in a manner compliant with YouTube’s Terms of

 5   Service. When YouTube has expressed specific concerns to Musi about the app’s functionality,

 6   Musi has, in good faith, either adjusted the app’s functionality or provided detailed explanations

 7   of how the app works and why it complies with YouTube’s Terms of Service. In April 2021,

 8   YouTube’s outside counsel raised several questions regarding the Musi app’s functionality. Musi

 9   promptly responded with a substantive explanation, but YouTube never replied. Nearly two years
10   later, in March 2023, YouTube sent a complaint notification to Apple about the Musi app, stating
11   only “YouTube TOS Violations.” Musi again promptly responded to Apple, referring back to its
12   2021 communications and the lack of response, but YouTube remained silent.
13           Apple’s ultimate removal of the Musi app from the App Store was preceded by a
14   coordinated effort to generate a basis for Musi’s removal at the behest of certain music-industry
15   players. For years, several music industry organizations—including the National Music Publishers
16   Association (NMPA), the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI), Universal
17   Music Group (UMG), Sony Music Entertainment (SME), and the Recording Industry Association
18   of America (RIAA)—had lodged complaints with Apple regarding the Musi app through the
19   Apple’s form app dispute process. Musi responded to such complaints, and they never resulted in
20   the app’s removal.
21           In or around April 2024, the approach from the music industry changed. Rather than filing
22   formal complaints through Apple’s established process, at least one music industry player began
23   to pressure Apple directly, expressly seeking its help to secure the permanent removal of the Musi
24   app. Specifically, Sony Music, through Jeff Walker, complained to Apple that its previous
25   attempts to remove Musi via the app dispute process had failed. This company also informed
26   Apple that Google had taken measures to block Musi from using YouTube’s API, undermining
27

28
      Case No. 5:24-cv-06920-EKL                     3                  JOINT CASE MANAGEMENT STATEMENT
               Case 5:24-cv-06920-EKL          Document 91        Filed 07/16/25      Page 4 of 18




 1   the basis for YouTube’s later claim that Musi was violating YouTube’s API Terms of Service (and

 2   Musi had also stated, in prior emails years earlier copying Apple, that it did not use YouTube’s

 3   API). Sony Music specifically requested Apple’s assistance in removing the Musi app.

 4            Apple, presumably recognizing the legal risk of removing a popular app without a clear

 5   basis, did not immediately comply. Instead, Apple began a “backchannel scheme” to create the

 6   appearance of a legitimate reason for removal. Specifically, Apple proactively reached out to

 7   YouTube, encouraging it to “reopen” a previously dormant, 14-month-old complaint that Apple

 8   had previously treated as resolved due to YouTube’s total lack of response to messages from Apple

 9   about the complaint. Apple and YouTube held a July 15, 2024, telephone conference in which the
10   Musi app was discussed. Witness testimony and contemporary notes confirm that, during that call,
11   YouTube explained that the basis for its complaint was an alleged violation of the YouTube API.
12   After that call, Apple sent YouTube its prior complaint and invited YouTube to respond if it
13   wanted to re-open its complaint.
14            Apple also received (and on information and belief, likely solicited) a letter of support from
15   the NMPA, which purported to provide “evidence” that Musi was violating YouTube’s API Terms
16   of Service. Notably, Apple did not share this NMPA letter with Musi until litigation commenced
17   (and only then via filings in this litigation), and the letter itself contained several factual
18   inaccuracies (including the claim that the Musi app was using YouTube’s API, which—again—
19   Apple already knew to be false based on previously provided information from both Sony and
20   Musi).
21            On August 8, 2024, Apple informed Musi that it had received a notice from “YouTube
22   Legal” stating that the Musi app “infringes its intellectual property rights” and “violating YouTube
23   Terms of Service,” but provided no further details. Musi’s outside counsel responded four days
24   later, explaining that the accusations were unsubstantiated and, in reference to the 2021
25   communication with YouTube’s counsel, that Musi had previously attempted to resolve the dispute
26   directly with YouTube. On September 6, 2024, YouTube emailed Apple and inaccurately claimed
27

28
      Case No. 5:24-cv-06920-EKL                        4                   JOINT CASE MANAGEMENT STATEMENT
             Case 5:24-cv-06920-EKL          Document 91        Filed 07/16/25      Page 5 of 18




 1   that Musi had never initiated contact to resolve the dispute. Musi’s counsel responded to correct

 2   the record and reiterated that the Musi app did not infringe YouTube’s intellectual property or

 3   violate its Terms of Service, and again invited YouTube to discuss its concerns. Musi received no

 4   response.

 5           Having heard nothing further from either YouTube or Apple, Musi’s counsel followed up

 6   with Apple on September 19 and again on September 24, 2024, updating Apple that Musi had yet

 7   to receive any communication from YouTube in response to Musi’s September 6 correspondence.

 8   Apple responded by stating, without acknowledging Musi’s prior communications, that “your app

 9   will be removed from the App Store on the basis of intellectual property infringement.” Apple
10   removed the Musi app that same day. Notably, at no time during the discussions in 2024 did Apple
11   ever state or suggest that its removal of the Musi app was based on complaints from any entity
12   other than YouTube. Nor did Apple share with Musi that it had been engaged in discussions with
13   other entities about the Musi app, the nature of those discussions, or the nature of any claims made
14   about the Musi app in the course of such discussions.
15           Apple justified its decision by citing Schedule 1 § 6.3, Schedule 2 § 7.3, and Schedule 3 §
16   7.3 of its Developer Agreement with Musi. However, as set forth in Musi’s First Amended
17   Complaint, Apple did not comply with the Developer Agreement’s requirements, including the

 3           Musi owns and operates the Musi – Simple Music Streaming app (the “Musi app”). The

 4   Musi app allows users to access content from YouTube through Musi’s own augmented interface,

 5   which replaces YouTube’s advertising content with Musi’s own advertisements to generate

 6   revenue. While the Musi app was on the App Store, the app was free to download, though users

 7   could also pay a one-time fee for ad-free streaming. Since launching in or around 2013, the app

 8   has amassed millions of users. Musi does not share any of its revenue with YouTube or any of the

 9   artists, musicians, or other copyright holders whose music or songs are streamed using the Musi
10   app.
11           Musi has been in conversation with YouTube about the Musi app and its compliance with
12   YouTube’s Terms of Service since at least 2015. In April 2021, outside counsel for YouTube
13   identified several specific concerns YouTube had with the Musi app’s functionality, including the

15   advertising. Musi disputed YouTube’s understanding of the Musi app’s functionality, but Musi
16   and YouTube did not reach a final resolution regarding YouTube’s concerns. In March 2023,
17   Apple received a complaint from YouTube that the Musi app infringes YouTube’s intellectual
18   property rights—specifically, its Terms of Service. Apple shared this complaint with Musi, and
19   Musi responded that the complaint was unsubstantiated, but the complaint otherwise went
20   unresolved.

22   the email chain—falsely represented to Apple that Musi had been in communication directly with
23   YouTube to attempt to come to a timely resolution of their dispute. In fact, despite outside
24   counsel’s representations that Musi was currently communicating with YouTube regarding the
25   complaint submitted in 2023, there were no communications between Musi or its counsel and
26   YouTube in March or April 2023. On April 19, 2023, Apple wrote YouTube, copying Musi, to

 1   I.      INTRODUCTION

 2           Musi’s Opposition confirms that material allegations in the First Amended Complaint

 3   (FAC), filed after Musi had the opportunity to take discovery, lack evidentiary support in violation

 4   of Fed. R. Civ. P. 11(b)(3). Musi attempts to sidestep most of its misrepresentations and offers

 5   insufficient support for those it chooses to confront. Musi had ample opportunity to withdraw

 6   these allegations, which are the lynchpin of its baseless bad faith claim, and cannot evade sanctions

 7   by pretending they do not exist. Apple’s motion for sanctions should be granted.

 8   II.     ARGUMENT

 9           A.      Musi Fails To Support The Fabricated “Admission” Featured In The FAC
10           The first paragraph of Musi’s FAC claims that Apple relied on evidence submitted by the
11   National Music Publishers Association when it removed Musi’s app even though “Apple knew
12   that this ‘evidence’ was false, as it has since admitted[.]” FAC ¶ 1. Musi provisionally redacted
13   this allegation, misleadingly suggesting that it reflected discovery material. Dkt. 62. But, as Apple
14   demonstrated, there is no evidentiary support whatsoever for this alleged “admission”—no Apple
15   witness ever “admitted” that Apple “knew” that “evidence” relied upon by Apple in removing
16   Musi’s app was “false.” See Mot. at 7. Notably, after emphasizing this alleged “admission” in the
17   opening paragraph of its FAC, Musi does not even try to defend it in its opposition brief.
18           Instead, Musi employs a strategy of misdirection, pivoting to an argument that “Musi’s
19   allegations that Apple knew by July 2024 that the Musi app was not using YouTube’s API are also
20   well supported,” and it is a “fact issue” about whether the “evidence is enough to show …
21   knowledge.” Opp. at 7. Of course, this is beside the point. The real “fact issue” is whether Musi
22   entirely invented an “admission” that does not exist. Unsurprisingly, Musi’s opposition fails to
23   identify any evidence that even tangentially supports the allegation that Apple “has since admitted”
24   that it “knew” evidence that it relied upon was false. See Opp. at 7 (citing to discovery discussing
25   what a third party represented to Apple). Having refused to withdraw this baseless allegation,
26   Musi cannot evade sanctions by ignoring it.
27

28

      Case No. 5:24-cv-06920-EKL                      1                     REPLY ISO MOTION FOR SANCTIONS
              Case 5:24-cv-06920-EKL          Document 88        Filed 06/05/25      Page 5 of 9




 1           B.      Musi Fails To Support The Fabricated YouTube “Disavowal”

 2           Key to Musi’s bad faith claim is its allegation that “[i]t was on [the July 15, 2024 call

 3   between YouTube and Apple] that YouTube supposedly stated to Apple that its complaint with

 4   Musi was not a violation of its user Terms of Service … but rather an unspecified violation of

 5   YouTube’s API Terms of Service.” FAC ¶ 46 (emphases added). Here, the word “supposedly”

 6   does the same work of the word “admitted” in the first paragraph of the FAC, suggesting that

 7   Musi’s allegation is somehow warranted by specific evidence produced in this case. Once again,

 8   Musi’s allegation has no evidentiary support and, once again, Musi fails to defend it.

 9           Musi again employs a pivot, arguing that it is improper for Apple to demand evidence that
10   YouTube “disavowed” a complaint under the user Terms. Opp. at 7. But a disavowal is precisely
11   what Musi alleged: YouTube “supposedly stated to Apple” that its complaint was “not a violation”
12   of those terms. Musi now admits that no evidence supports its allegation about what YouTube
13   “supposedly said” to Apple. Instead, Musi argues that YouTube cited to the API Terms during the
14   July 2024 call, and it is therefore reasonable to infer that YouTube was not raising a complaint
15   under the user Terms. But Musi did not allege an inference, it alleged that YouTube “supposedly
16   stated” something directly to Apple. It cannot avoid Rule 11 by pretending otherwise.
17           Moreover, the premise of Musi’s inference is itself lacking evidentiary support. Musi
18   stretches the testimony it cites, claiming that, as an Apple witness “repeatedly testified,” the
19   “specific basis YouTube gave for its complaint in July 2024 was violations of its ‘API guidelines,’”
20   Opp. at 6-7, when the only time the phrase “API guideline[s]” appears in the cited testimony is in
21   reference to the “original” complaint brought by YouTube, see Dkt. 83-10 at 52. The witness
22   elsewhere refers to “API issues” but testified that YouTube did not specify which provisions of
23   which terms were implicated by those issues. Id. at 96:20-22. And Musi inserts the word “API”
24   into a quote from contemporaneous notes of the call, making the sentence “there are some
25   violations” into “there are some [API] violations.” Opp. at 7.
26           Even if Musi had an evidentiary basis to allege that YouTube raised violations of the API
27   terms on the phone call, that evidence is plainly insufficient to support Musi’s allegation that
28   YouTube also disavowed a complaint under the user Terms. There is a wide range of conduct,

      Case No. 5:24-cv-06920-EKL                      2                     REPLY ISO MOTION FOR SANCTIONS
              Case 5:24-cv-06920-EKL          Document 88        Filed 06/05/25       Page 6 of 9




 1   including selling advertisements, modifying YouTube content, and accessing YouTube through

 2   unauthorized means, that violates both sets of terms. See Dkt. 68-9 at 7; Dkt. 30-7 at § 3G.1.a-d.

 3   Musi fails to identify any evidence that YouTube “supposedly stated” that its complaint was “not

 4   a violation” of the user Terms, and its allegation violates Rule 11.

 5           C.      Musi Fails To Defend Its Misrepresentations Of Specific Documents

 6           Musi’s opposition also ignores that the FAC misrepresents the content of documents,

 7   including the April 11, 2024 email from Sony Music Entertainment, see Mot. at 7 (highlighting

 8   that the document does not say, as Musi alleges it does, that “years earlier, Musi had ceased use

 9   of YouTube’s API” (FAC ¶ 44)), as well as Winston & Strawn emails to Apple in early 2023, see
10   Mot. at 6 (pointing out that the emails, see Dkt. 83-9, never “referenc[e Musi’s] previous detailed
11   letter from 2021” and do not say that Musi had “previously” been in touch with YouTube (FAC
12   ¶ 5)). Unable to defend the FAC’s allegations, Musi resorts to misdirection. Apple is not “argu[ing
13   that] Musi should be sanctioned for the wording of a pre-litigation April 2023 communication,”
14   Opp. at 5—rather, Apple argues that Musi and its counsel should be sanctioned because the
15   allegation about that communication in the FAC is false. And Apple argues that by falsely
16   describing those communications, Musi misleads the Court about why Apple “closed” YouTube’s
17   2023 complaint. Mot. at 6. Musi’s failure to defend the FAC’s misrepresentations is dispositive.
18           D.      Musi Fails To Support Its Allegations About Apple’s Outreach To YouTube
19           In contrast to the other challenged allegations, Musi has attempted to defend its allegations
20   about Apple’s outreach to YouTube, but falls short. As just one example, Musi alleges that Apple
21   reached out to YouTube to “goad” YouTube into action, but “[a]n immediate roadblock” to its
22   “plan” “became apparent” when “its contacts at YouTube had no idea what Apple was talking
23   about.” FAC ¶ 46. Musi cites testimony demonstrating that Apple’s initial outreach was to a
24   person who had never heard of Musi. Opp. at 5. But what Musi’s argument elides is that the initial
25   outreach from Ms. Singh, who has a non-legal role at Apple, to her counterpart at YouTube, who
26   also has a non-legal role, was for the purpose of asking him to arrange a call with the YouTube
27   legal team—who did know about YouTube’s complaint—so the Apple legal team could inquire
28   about its status. See Dkt. 86-4 at 76:1-10. And so it is throughout the FAC: Musi takes testimony

      Case No. 5:24-cv-06920-EKL                      3                      REPLY ISO MOTION FOR SANCTIONS
                 Case 5:24-cv-06920-EKL           Document 88        Filed 06/05/25      Page 7 of 9




 1   supporting an unremarkable fact (here, a single YouTube employee knew nothing about Musi) and

 2   then misrepresents that testimony (becoming Apple’s “contacts” (plural) at YouTube “had no idea

 3   what Apple was talking about”). Then Musi adds a host of embellishments that fundamentally

 4   change the meaning of the fact supported by the testimony.                  Here, leaving aside other

 5   misrepresentations about the outreach, the singular contact’s lack of personal knowledge obviously

 6   could not be an “immediate roadblock” that “became apparent” after Apple’s initial outreach

 7   unless Apple expected him to have knowledge about YouTube’s complaint and contacted him for

 8   the purpose of discussing the complaint with him. But there is no evidentiary support for those

 9   propositions, which are directly contrary to Ms. Singh’s testimony. Ex. 1 at 38:6-13, 39:9-40:21
10   (describing limited role of her single YouTube contact, with whom she “facilitate[d]
11   communications as necessary” regarding technical issues, e.g., “software bug[s]”). 1 Similar
12   embellishments permeate both the FAC and the opposition. See Mot. at 4-5. 2 As this Court has

13   made abundantly clear, misrepresentations of fact, even if “subtle,” are sanctionable. Standing

14   Order for Civil Cases, Section VIII.F.

15              E.      Musi’s Allegations About Other Complaints Are False And Misleading

16              In its opposition, Musi argues that it is not required to plead Apple’s defenses and so should

17   not be sanctioned for failing to allege other complaints about Musi, but Musi again fails to address

18   Apple’s challenge. See Opp. at 7-8. Apple challenged Musi’s allegation that members of the

19   music industry had raised complaints to Apple and those complaints “were ultimately closed.”

20   Mot. at 8 (citing FAC ¶ 7). As Musi and its counsel were well aware, and Musi does not deny in

21   its opposition, multiple complaints from members of the music industry had not been closed and

22   were active at the time of Musi’s removal. Musi violates Rule 11 because the FAC would

23   improperly cause any “reasonable person reading [it to] believe, contrary to the facts,” that no

24   complaints against Musi other than YouTube’s were pending at the time of removal. Lake v.

25   Gates, 130 F.4th 1064, 1069 (9th Cir. 2025). The FAC is littered with allegations like this,

26
     1
27    “Ex. 1” refers to Exhibit 1 to the concurrently filed Declaration of Jennifer Milici.
     2
      For example, YouTube’s inability to locate Apple’s 2023 email and request that it be re-sent
28   becomes “YouTube … could not be bothered to even look up its prior complaint.” FAC ¶ 47.

         Case No. 5:24-cv-06920-EKL                       4                     REPLY ISO MOTION FOR SANCTIONS
              Case 5:24-cv-06920-EKL           Document 88         Filed 06/05/25      Page 8 of 9




 1   designed to mislead the reader about the history of complaints and Musi’s conduct in responding

 2   to those complaints. See, e.g., FAC ¶¶ 3, 6, 7; Dkt. 83-3.

 3           F.      Musi’s Request For Sanctions Is Frivolous

 4           As set forth above, Musi makes no attempt to defend many of the challenged allegations,

 5   including its allegation that Apple “admitted” that it relied on evidence that it “knew” was false.

 6   Musi’s attempt to deflect attention from those false allegations by seeking sanctions against Apple

 7   should be rejected. There is nothing improper about bringing Rule 11 violations to the Court’s

 8   attention. Apple is not seeking to litigate the same issues it presents in its motion to dismiss, which

 9   argues that, even if all of the factual allegations are credited, Musi’s FAC must be dismissed
10   because the express terms of the contract preclude Musi’s claims. Here, in contrast, Apple argues
11   that Musi violated Rule 11 by making factual allegations that lack evidentiary support, which is
12   an entirely separate issue.
13           Apple’s sanctions motion is also not a premature summary judgment motion. Apple is not
14   asking the Court to determine that Musi lacks sufficient evidence to prove a claim. Rather, Apple
15   is challenging specific factual allegations under Rule 11(b)(3) because they lack evidentiary
16   support. Musi has failed to identify any factual basis for those allegations, and its cited authority
17   is inapposite. See Goldwater Bank, N.A. v. Elizarov, 2023 WL 4295255, at *4 (C.D. Cal. May 9,
18   2023) (imposing sanctions on defendant who essentially admitted “that his Rule 11 Motion was
19   the motion-equivalent of a mulligan and that it was a thinly veiled attempt to relitigate his denied
20   motion to dismiss”); Williamson v. Basco, 2007 WL 9711043, at *2-3 (D. Haw. Aug. 21, 2007)
21   (imposing sanctions because pro se plaintiff failed to comply with the safe harbor provision and
22   because Rule 11 does not apply to statements made in initial disclosures).
23   III.    CONCLUSION
24           For the foregoing reasons, and for the reasons set forth in Apple’s opening brief, Apple
25   respectfully requests that the Court grant Apple’s motion for sanctions pursuant to Rule 11(c) of
26   the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.
27

28

 1   I.     INTRODUCTION
 2          Apple’s Rule 11 motion is frivolous, and this Court should deny it and impose sanctions on

 3   Apple for its improper motion. Rule 11 is too often used as a “tactic of intimidation and harassment” in

 4   “so-called ‘hardball’ litigation techniques.” arrivia Inc. v. Rowley, 2024 WL 3010935, at *5 (D. Ariz.

 5   June 14, 2024) (quoting Gaiardo v. Ethyl Corp., 835 F.2d 479, 485 (3d Cir. 1987)). Unfortunately,

 6   Apple’s motion is a member of that shameful lineage. As Musi already explained to Apple’s counsel in

 7   a detailed letter with cites to supporting evidence, every one of Musi’s allegations that Apple asserts

 8   lacks supporting evidence in fact has support. Declaration of Jennifer A. Golinveaux (“Golinveaux

 9   Decl.”),1 Ex. 1, Musi’s April 25, 2025 Correspondence. Apple’s filing of its Rule 11 motion despite

10   Musi’s detailed showing is not only baseless, but frivolous and abusive. As shown below, none of

11   Musi’s challenged allegations are factually baseless, and all are based on a reasonable and competent

12   inquiry by Musi’s counsel. Apple’s motion should thus be denied, and Apple should itself be sanctioned

13   and required to pay Musi’s attorneys’ fees for opposing its baseless motion.

14   II.    LEGAL STANDARD
15          Rule 11 sanctions for filing a complaint may be ordered only if (1) the “complaint is legally or

16   factually ‘baseless’ from an objective perspective” and (2) the attorney failed to conduct a “‘reasonable

17   and competent inquiry’ before signing and filing” the complaint. Christian v. Mattel, Inc., 286 F.3d

18   1118, 1127 (9th Cir. 2002) (quoting Buster v. Greisen, 104 F.3d 1186, 1190 (9th Cir. 1997)). Sanctions

19   are appropriate “based upon factual assertions” only when “the factual allegations were completely

20   unwarranted by the evidence.” U.S. ex rel. Jacobs v. Advanced Dermatology & Skin Cancer Specialists,

21   P.C., 2023 WL 6370921, at *5 (C.D. Cal. Aug. 24, 2023) (citation omitted). Conversely, sanctions are

22   not appropriate if there is even “some credible evidence” in support of a party’s statements. Himaka v.

23   Buddhist Churches of Am., 917 F. Supp. 698, 710 (N.D. Cal. 1995) (citation omitted); see also Frost v.

24   LG Elecs. Inc., 2017 WL 2775041, at *3 (N.D. Cal. June 27, 2017). Moreover, “circumstantial evidence,

25   and the reasonable inferences drawn from that evidence, are treated as evidentiary support” for purposes

26   of Rule 11. In re Cal. Bail Bond Antitrust Litig., 511 F. Supp. 3d 1031, 1053–54 (N.D. Cal. 2021)

 5           “Rule 11(b) states that, by ‘signing, filing, submitting or later advocating’ for a ‘pleading,
 6   written motion, or other paper,’ an attorney certifies that:”
 7           (1) it is not presented for any improper purpose, such as to harass, cause
             unnecessary delay, or needlessly increase the cost of litigation; (2) the claims,
 8           defenses, and other legal contentions are warranted by existing law or by a
 9           nonfrivolous argument for extending, modifying, or reversing existing law or for

10           if specifically so identified, will likely have evidentiary support after a reasonable
             opportunity for further investigation or discovery[.]
11

12

14

15

16

17

20

22
     1153 (9th Cir. 2002). Misleading “omi[ssions of] critical information” that “directly contradict[]”

 8           The claims in the FAC are a repeat of the express breach and implied covenant contract

 9   claims brought in Musi’s initial complaint. Compare FAC ¶¶ 60-71 with Dkt. 1 ¶¶ 43-54. Yet

10   this Court has already held, citing to well-established case law, that “[b]ased on the plain language

11   of the [contracts], Apple had the express right to remove the Musi app from the App Store ‘at any

12   time, with or without cause’ … [and t]he covenant of good faith and fair dealing cannot impose an

13   obligation on Apple that contradicts this express term.” Dkt. 44 at 14 (citing cases). Thus, even

14   if the FAC were supported by well-pled factual allegations (which it is not), given the Court’s clear

15   application of established California law regarding contract interpretation and the permissible

16   scope of implied covenant claims, Musi’s counsel cannot “establish[] that it was reasonable to

17   believe, following a reasonable inquiry, that [Musi’s] claims had merit, as required under Rule

18   11(b)(2).” Ramachandran v. City of Los Altos, 2024 WL 3364021, at *7 (N.D. Cal. July 9, 2024).

20   August 2019 that Musi “appreciate[s] that Apple has a contractual right to remove apps from the
